title: Strength in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7–10)
hookLine: a thorn in the flesh, and my grace is sufficient for thee

lines: CAUGHT UP TO THE THIRD HEAVEN.
THEN PAUL BOASTS OF A WOUND.
cards: Paul's critics in Corinth liked credentials: visions, revelations, impressive speech. So Paul plays their game, reluctantly.
He knows a man, he says, who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven and heard words no one may speak. A few verses on, it's clear the man is Paul himself.

It's the kind of story his rivals would have loved to tell. And just as they lean in, Paul stops boasting about visions and starts boasting about something else entirely: a wound he couldn't get rid of.

teach.h: A STING, A THORN, A STAKE.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims he calls it "a sting of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me." The King James calls it a thorn in the flesh. The Greek word, skolops, can mean a splinter or a sharpened stake.
Nobody knows, and Paul never says.
Readers have guessed for centuries: an eye disease, since he mentions writing in large letters; malaria; migraines; epilepsy; a stammer; the opponents who dogged him; a temptation he couldn't shake.
The silence may be a mercy: anyone can put their own thorn in that space. What Paul does tell us is what he did.
Three times he asked the Lord to take it away. The answer was not yes.

It was this: "My grace is sufficient for thee; for power is made perfect in infirmity." Paul turns the boasting upside down: "Gladly therefore will I glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me."
The Greek for dwell is a word about pitching a tent: Christ's power camps where Paul is weakest. Then the line the whole passage has been building to: "For when I am weak, then am I powerful."
Catholics have found company here. Some of the Church's saints lived with illness, pain and limits that never lifted. The Church doesn't call suffering good in itself, and it prays for healing.
But it holds that a weakness offered to God is not wasted. The thorn stayed.

teach.h: MY GRACE IS SUFFICIENT FOR THEE.

how: Catholics speak of "offering up" a suffering, uniting it to Christ's; the Church also prays for healing, and offers the anointing of the sick to those who are seriously ill.

games.q: you're Paul. you've begged three times for the thorn to go, and it hasn't. what do you do next?
o: stop praying and hide the weakness.
glory in your infirmities, so Christ's power may dwell in you.
decide the visions were never real.
games.why: "gladly therefore will I glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me."

practice: Name, quietly, in a word or two, one weakness you carry that hasn't gone away, however much you've wished it would: a body that hurts, a temper, anxiety, a loss. Don't analyze it or fix it; just notice how heavy it feels.
If you pray, say Paul's answer back to God, my grace is sufficient, and stay with it; if not, notice that you're still here, carrying it.

wordCard.voice: Skolops. The thorn Paul couldn't get rid of, and the answer he got instead of its removal: my grace is sufficient for thee. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a splinter or a sharpened stake. KJV 'thorn', Douay-Rheims 'sting' (2 Corinthians 12:7).
